In [[mathematics]], more specifically [[general topology]], the '''nested interval topology''' is an example of a topology given to the [[open interval]] (0,1), i.e. the [[set (mathematics)|set]] of all [[real number]]s ''x'' such that {{nowrap|1=0 < ''x'' < 1}}. The open interval (0,1) is the set of all real numbers ''between'' 0 and 1; but ''not including'' either 0 or 1.

To give the set (0,1) a topology means to say which [[subset]]s of (0,1) are "open", and to do so in a way that the following [[axiom]]s are met:<ref name="CEIT">{{Citation|first=L. A.|last=Steen|first2=J. A.|last2=Seebach|title=[[Counterexamples in Topology]]|publisher=Dover|year=1995|ISBN=0-486-68735-X}}</ref>

# The [[union (mathematics)|union]] of open sets is an open set.
# The finite [[intersection (mathematics)|intersection]] of open sets is an open set.
# The set (0,1) and the [[empty set]] ∅ are open sets.

== Construction ==

The set (0,1) and the empty set ∅ are required to be open sets, and so we define (0,1) and ∅ to be open sets in this topology. The other open sets in this topology are all of the form {{nowrap|1=(0,1 − 1/''n'')}} where ''n'' is a positive [[Natural number|whole number]] greater than or equal to two i.e. {{nowrap|1=''n'' = 2, 3, 4, 5, ...}}.<ref name="CEIT"/>

== Properties ==

* The nested interval topology is neither [[Hausdorff topology|Hausdorff]] nor [[T1 space|T1]]. In fact, if ''x'' is an element of (0,1), then the [[closure (topology)|closure]] of the [[singleton set]] {''x''} is the [[Interval (mathematics)#Including or excluding endpoints|half-open interval]] {{nowrap|1=[1 − 1/''n'',1)}}, where ''n'' is maximal such that {{nowrap|1=''n'' ≤ (1 − ''x'')<sup>−1</sup>}}.<ref name="CEIT"/>
* The nested interval topology is not [[compact space|compact]]. It is, however, [[Lindelof space|strongly Lindelöf]] since there are only countably many open sets.<ref name="CEIT"/>
* The nested interval topology is [[Irreducible space|hyperconnected]] and hence [[Connected space|connected]].<ref name="CEIT"/>
* The nested interval topology is [[Alexandrov topology|Alexandrov]].<ref name="CEIT"/>
